text: In Livingstone, Zambia, community members commonly engage in testifying about the nyami nyami god, a mysterious river deity they deeply believe in. This cultural practice is widely regarded as a normative behavior within the sampled population, reflecting the strong influence of traditional beliefs and spirituality in the region. The act of testifying about the nyami nyami god serves as a significant aspect of their cultural identity and belief system, showcasing the profound reverence and faith community members hold for this enigmatic river god. This practice is deeply ingrained in the cultural fabric of the community, reflecting the enduring significance of traditional spiritual beliefs in their daily lives.

In Livingstone, near Victoria Falls and Zambia, community members and the organization Beyond Zambia actively engage in learning experiences, share cultural knowledge, and participate in local traditions with the goal of understanding and preserving Zambian culture and beliefs. This inclusive approach extends to both community members and tourists, who are encouraged to participate in cultural exchange activities. The involvement of Zambia Tourism further emphasizes the commitment to promoting cultural understanding and preservation. This behavior is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, reflecting a strong consensus on the importance of cultural exchange and preservation in the Zambian context.

In the Zambian educational context, students typically follow a structured system of 7 years of primary education followed by 5 years of secondary education, which is further divided into 3 terms per year. This educational framework is widely regarded as the norm within the Zambian cultural group, with a significant portion of the sampled population agreeing that this system is standard. The consistency and universality of this educational structure reflect its high level of normativity within the Zambian cultural context.

In Zambian households and social gatherings, it is customary for men, especially fathers, to eat and handle chicken gizzard, as it is considered reserved for men. This behavior is particularly gender-based, with women and children being the recipients. It is expected that the recipients, especially women and children, may touch the gizzard, but the primary handling and consumption are reserved for men. This practice is perceived as moderately normative within the sampled population, indicating that it is neither universally accepted nor widely controversial.

Most people tend to follow a very indirect form of communicating. One Zambian described her fellow citizens are being "conciliatory", which tends to be a very apt description. People will almost never say no flat out; in no's place you may find an exaggerated pause, or something to that effect. People avoid having to be brutally honest, instead choosing to broach sensitive topics by referring to them in the metaphorical sense, or the third person, as it is removed from those communicating. Avoid asking about HIV/AIDS as there tends to be somewhat of a social stigma related to it.

Generally speaking, an arm’s length or a bit less of personal space is appropriate during conversations. Personal space tends to be less between members of the same gender. When two people of the same sex are talking, light touching is acceptable. It is common for two men (or two women) to walk hand in hand in public. This does not have any implication on their sexual preferences; it's just a sign of friendship and closeness. For women, it is best not to touch a man during conversations because he may take it to mean that you are interested in him. This may be different between good friends and family members. There is little to no touching during initial and business meetings; this is especially true between a superior and subordinates. Touching, expect between friends of the same sex, is seen as very significant and should be avoided. Public displays of affection like kissing or hugging in public are usually considered to be sexually explicit and to be avoided.

Indirect eye contact is very important. When a young person looks an elder in the eyes it is usually seen as disrespectful. In many situations, i f a woman looks a man in the eye she is thought to be flirting with him. Between equals of the same sex there is usually no problem with making direct eye contact.

While people tend to be more punctual in business settings vs. social ones, deadlines are often not met and it is common for meetings to start 1-2 hours after the time they have been called for. Generally speaking, people give their time freely and tend to live in the present rather than the future. People often refer to time my motioning where the sun will be. So later in the afternoon will be indicated by an arm extended to the west. Buses do not usually adhere to schedules. Instead they wait until being full to leave.

Generally speaking, women in the villages aren’t considered equal to men even though they do a bulk of the work at the homestead and in the fields. This tends to be the case in urban environments as well. Women are primary care givers for the entire family/community. They rarely consume alcohol, or wear slacks. Especially in rural areas.

Beckoning someone with a single index finger (raised and bended towards you) is considered to be very rude. It is usually only used when calling an animal, like a dog. Most people beckon one another with the palm facing out and moving their fingers back and forth in a scratching motion. Avoid beckoning someone by whistling as it is reserved for animals. Avoid touching someone on the head as it can be seen as mocking them. This tends to be reserved for children.

Not greeting at the beginning of any interaction is considered very rude. Appropriate dress is very important; for example men/women in shorts is seen as sloppy. Any sloppiness is noticed and considered rude. Women, except in very urban settings, should never expose their thighs. All skirts and trousers should fall below the knee. Avoid beckoning someone by whistling as it is reserved for animals. Avoid touching someone on the head as it can be seen as mocking them. This tends to be reserved for children. Avoid asking about HIV/AIDS as there tends to be somewhat of a social stigma related to it. Public displays of affection like kissing or hugging in public are usually considered to be sexually explicit and to be avoided.

The legal drinking and smoking age is 18 and is not heavily enforced. A "Clean Up Zambia" Act has been passed recently which prohibits the following in public: smoking, urinating, sex, bicycle riding in markets, etc. These laws are strongly enforced and there have been foreigners arrested for breaking them Penalties for possession, use, or trafficking in illegal drugs in are severe, and convicted offenders can expect long jail sentences and heavy fines.

For Men - Nice slacks and button down shirts. Suits may be required in some industries, but are usually reserved for formal events. For Women - Many Zambian women wear traditional chitenje suits. For foreigners, a formal blouse (no shoulders exposed) and skirt or slacks which cover the knees is the way to go. Conservative attire is appropriate in most situations. Jeans and less causal attire (shorts especially) are not appropriate for business situations. Clean well pressed clothing is very important. If someone is under dressed or dressed like a slob it could change the way they are treated.

Titles are important, especially when dealing with members of the government. It is best to use a title plus the surname when calling someone by name and wait to be invited to call someone by their first name. It is best to hand business cards with the right hand while holding your forearm with your left hand.

People are usually formally introduced at the beginning of the meetings and then there is someone chosen to lead the meeting. Business meetings may not begin on time, however it is a good idea for a foreigner to be punctual. It's important to greet the most senior individuals first. Small talk almost always precedes any formal conversations. It's appropriate to inquire about one's health, families, etc., before dealing with business. T he "get to the point" mentality is usually seen as rude. Setting a friendly mood will get you a lot further than trying to be direct about anything.

Bargaining is acceptable in most situations and it is best to remain calm. Decisions tend to come from the top down and may take awhile to be reached. When negotiating it's customary to greet the seller in one of the many local languages (preferably Nyanga since everyone speaks it), but usually the first offer will be outrageous, so you would probably want to bargain down to half or lower on any price they give you, in the market. Bargaining is expected at markets. It's best to always appear friendly, but don't back down. If all else fails walk away. Be sure to shop around before settling on something. Inevitably there will be 10 people or more selling the same exact items.
May not give gifts to government officials as it may make them feel embarrassed. A few small gifts with your company logo will be welcome.

이들 기관은 미국 보건부의 에이즈 구호 계획(PEPFAR)의 지원을 받아 교육 프로그램을 운영하며, 콜롬비아대학교 등 같은 미국 교육 기관과도 협력하여 간호 9 치텡게는 잠비아 여성들이 즐겨 입는 전통 의상으로 다채로운 색상과 복잡한 무늬가 특징임. 스커트, 드레스, 머리띠 등 다양한 형태가 있음 68 Republic of Zambia 잠비아 개황 69 Ⅶ 사회 문화 Ⅷ 한-잠비아 관계 한-잠비아 외교장관 회담(2024 한-아프리카 정상회의 계기) 70 Republic of Zambia 잠비아 개황 71 1. 정의화 국회의장 2 016년 한-아프리카 농식품 기술협력협의체(KAFACI: Korea-Africa Food and Agriculture Cooperation Initiative)에 잠비아 합류 2 022.
